title: Love unreturned
hook: love that isn't returned is still love

segments.voice: Yesterday, love that lets go: the father who divided his living and watched the road. Your line was let go, lovingly. Where did you open your hand? Today closes a week of loving real people, and ends on a hard one. Day eight hundred sixty-eight.

A text sits on a phone with one small word under it, read, and a time stamp. No reply. An hour later, still nothing. A day later, still nothing. Some loves go like that. A crush that never turned around. A parent who couldn't say it back. A friend who drifted while you kept reaching. There's a woman in the book of Genesis who lived it, and the text gives her the words to say it. Her name is Leah. Today: love unreturned.
screen: `READ, AND NO REPLY.` → `SOME LOVES GO LIKE THAT.` → `A WOMAN NAMED LEAH.`

segments.voice: First, the setup. Jacob loves Rachel. He works for her father to marry her, and on the wedding night the father swaps in her older sister, Leah. Jacob marries Rachel too, and Genesis says it plainly: he "loved also Rachel more than Leah." So Leah lives inside a marriage where the love runs one way. Second, her words. When Leah's first son is born, she names him and says, in the King James text: "Surely the LORD hath looked upon my affliction; now therefore my husband will love me." Now he'll love me. With the sons that follow, the text keeps her hoping out loud: that the LORD has heard her, that her husband will be joined to her. Genesis doesn't hurry past her hope. It lets her say it, son after son. Third, the turn. With another son, her words change. "Now will I praise the LORD." No mention of Jacob this time. Nothing in the story says he suddenly loves her back. What changes is where Leah stands. Her love hasn't been returned, and she sets it down, not by hating anyone, but by turning toward praise. Fourth, a line from the apostle Paul that fits her. In his letter to the Corinthians, love, which the King James Bible calls charity, "seeketh not her own." Love that isn't paid back is not a failed transaction. In Paul's description, love was never a transaction to begin with. Christians and Jews read Leah's story in their own ways, and some readers see in her a quiet strength. Either way, the text gives an unreturned love its full weight, and calls it what it was.
screen: `HE LOVED RACHEL MORE THAN LEAH.` · `NOW MY HUSBAND WILL LOVE ME.` · `NOW WILL I PRAISE THE LORD.` · `LOVE SEEKETH NOT HER OWN.` · then, large: `LOVE UNRETURNED.`

segments.voice: This week has turned to parents, children, strangers, animals, the earth, and people who had to be let go. Now let the breath settle. Bring to mind one love that wasn't returned, old or recent, small or large. Don't argue with it, and don't reopen the case. Just let it be what it was. Say inwardly: that was love. If anger comes, let it pass by like weather. If you pray, you can hold that love in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Love unreturned. Love that went out and didn't come back, like Leah's, and still counts as love. Today's word.
Your line: still love. Today, when you remember someone who didn't love you back, try calling it what it was, love, instead of calling it a mistake. Day eight hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Jews and Christians read Leah's story in Genesis as scripture, and some teachers read it as a portrait of unanswered love and of a turn toward praise; Christians also read Paul's words on love in 1 Corinthians 13 as scripture.

myth: in Genesis, Jacob comes to love Leah more than Rachel
the text says he loved Rachel more than Leah, and doesn't say that changed.
Leah's words shift from hoping for Jacob's love to praising the LORD
with a later son she says, "now will I praise the LORD."
the King James Bible calls love charity in 1 Corinthians 13
charity is the KJV's word there: "seeketh not her own."

fork.setup: you're Leah. another son is born, and your husband still loves your sister more. what do you say?
options: now my husband will finally love me.
now will I praise the LORD.
fork.reveal: this time she doesn't mention Jacob: "now will I praise the LORD." the story never says he changed. Leah did.

original.note: Greek: love, the word Paul uses in 1 Corinthians 13, which the King James Bible renders charity.

trapdoor: what you thought: love that isn't returned was a waste.
what it means: love that goes out without coming back is still love, and can be set down without bitterness.
what a scholar hears: Genesis voices Leah's hope in her own words, then lets her turn to praise; Paul's agape seeketh not her own.
